title: Make Me a Holy Place
sum: On the mountain God begins the longest speech in the book. He asks Israel for a freely given offering of gold, silver, bronze, dyed yarn, linen, wood, oil, spices and gems, so that they can make him a holy place and he can live among them (25:8). Then he describes, in order of holiness, the first three furnishings: the ark of the testimony with its gold atonement lid and two cherubim, the place where God will meet Moses and speak (25:22); the table for the Presence Bread; and the gold lampstand shaped like a flowering almond tree.

The chapter turns from the covenant of chapter 24 to its purpose. God has rescued Israel and given them his law; now he wants to move in. Everything is to be made by the "pattern" Moses is shown on the mountain (25:9, 40), a phrase that has fed both Jewish and Christian thinking about a heavenly sanctuary of which the earthly one is a copy.
readings: Read as a blueprint

Read for its plain sense, the chapter is a set of building instructions for a portable shrine, with measurements in cubits and materials a people leaving Egypt could have carried. Readers who take it this way compare Egyptian portable chests carried on poles and gold-covered wooden furniture like that of Tutankhamun's tomb.
Read as a picture of heaven

Read through 25:9 and 25:40, the chapter describes a copy of something Moses saw: God's own throne room, with the ark as his footstool and the cherubim as his attendants. The rabbis spoke of a heavenly sanctuary facing the earthly one, and Hebrews 8:5 quotes 25:40 to argue that the tent was a shadow of the real sanctuary in heaven.

views.H: A real tent made at Sinai from the wealth the Israelites carried out of Egypt (12:35–36). The materials, techniques and design fit the second millennium BC: acacia wood grows in Sinai, gold overlay and poles for carrying are known from Egyptian shrines, and portable sanctuaries existed among desert peoples.
views.M: The chapter may preserve memories of a real tent shrine and a real chest for the ark (the ark is well attested in Samuel), elaborated in priestly tradition into a richer and more symmetrical structure than any group in the desert would have built.
views.C: Part of the Priestly source (P). Many critics date P to the exile or soon after; an Israeli school (Kaufmann, Haran, Milgrom, Knohl, and Hurvitz on the evidence of its Hebrew) dates it before the exile. Either way the design reflects the Jerusalem temple and priestly ideals: holiness rising in stages, precious metals graded by distance from the ark, and God present but invisible. Its purpose is to describe how God can live among a people, not to record a building project.
views.J: The weekly reading Terumah ("offering") begins here. The rabbis taught that each furnishing carried meaning: the ark the Torah, the table prosperity, the lampstand wisdom. Rashi and Ramban disagree on when this was commanded (see the note on 31:18). The verse "I will live in their midst," not "in it," became a saying that God dwells in each person who makes room for him.
views.X: Christians have read the ark and its lid as pictures of Christ: Paul calls Jesus the hilastērion, the Greek word for the atonement lid (Romans 3:25); the table points to the bread of life and the lampstand to the light of the world (John 6:35; 8:12). Hebrews 8:5 reads the "pattern" as the heavenly reality Christ entered.

deep.b: The instructions of chapters 25–31 come in seven speeches, each opening "The LORD said to Moses" (25:1; 30:11; 30:17; 30:22; 30:34; 31:1; 31:12). The seventh is about the Sabbath. Many scholars, among them Peter Kearney, Joseph Blenkinsopp, Moshe Weinfeld and Jon Levenson, have argued that this is deliberate: the making of God's house is told on the pattern of the making of the world in Genesis 1, which also has seven sections ending with the seventh day. The parallel continues at the end of the book (see 39:32, 39:43 and 40:33). Others think the seven speeches are simply where editors joined units together, and warn against seeing patterns too easily.

Builders begin with the walls; God begins with the ark. The instructions start at the center, the ark and its lid in the most holy place, and move outward: table and lampstand (25:23–40), then the tent itself (26), then the courtyard and its altar (27). The order is theological, from God's throne out to the people. When Bezalel builds, he starts with the tent and then the ark (36:8–37:9), the practical order. Rashi (on 38:22) and the Talmud (Berakhot 55a) already noticed the difference, and the rabbis drew from it that Bezalel understood the work better than Moses had explained it.

deep.title: A God who asks
deep.body: My own observation: the first thing God says about the sanctuary is not a command to build but a request for gifts, and only from "each person whose heart urges him on" (25:2). The God who brought Egypt to its knees by force will not live in a house built by force. Twelve chapters later the people bring so much that Moses has to stop them (36:5–7). The tabernacle is the one building in the Bible described as made entirely of gifts, which may be part of why its story ends with God filling it. Others have made similar observations: Childs, Fretheim and Sarna all contrast the willing gifts with the forced labor of Egypt and the demanded gold of the calf.

echoes: Exodus 24:15–18; Exodus 37:1–24; Leviticus 24:1–9; Numbers 7:89; 1 Samuel 4:4; 1 Kings 8:6–9; Zechariah 4:1–14; Romans 3:25; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:1–5; Revelation 1:12–20; Revelation 11:19

settings.what: The call for gifts and the pattern
settings.to: Moses, to tell the Israelites
settings.when: On the mountain, during the forty days (24:18)
settings.why: To ask for a gift from everyone whose heart urges them on: metals, yarn, skins, wood, oil, spices and stones. With them Israel will make a holy place, and God will live among them. It must be built exactly by the pattern shown to Moses. It opens the first of seven speeches (25:1; 30:11, 17, 22, 34; 31:1, 12). It binds no one to give; it asks the willing. The problem it answers is the book's great question: how can the holy God of the mountain go with his people?
settings.readers: For Israel the freewill gifts of former slaves, carrying Egypt's silver and gold, built God's home. Every later temple looked back to this pattern.
views: Traditional readers, and scholars such as Kitchen, Homan and Fleming, take it as a portable desert sanctuary like the great tents of Egyptian kings and of Mari.
A Priestly source before the exile
Yehezkel Kaufmann, Menahem Haran and Jacob Milgrom date the Priestly source (P) before the exile. Haran sees in the tabernacle a picture of the First Temple of Jerusalem.
A model for the Second Temple
Many other critical scholars think the Priestly writers shaped it during or after the exile, as an ideal for the Second Temple.
Jewish and Christian readers see it as a copy of a heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 8:5).

settings.what: Instructions for the ark, the lid, the table and the lampstand
settings.to: Moses, and through him the craftsmen who will build
settings.when: On the mountain
settings.why: To describe the holiest furnishings from the inside out. The ark holds the testimony. On it sits the gold atonement lid with two cherubim, where God will meet Moses and speak with him. Then come the table for the Presence Bread and the lampstand. The instructions bind the craftsmen to make them exactly, and later the priests who tend them in the holy place. The order answers how holiness is shown: by nearness to the ark.
settings.readers: For Israel the lid with its cherubim made the ark God's throne or footstool. So Israel knew its God as enthroned but unseen, with no image.

title: Curtains, Frames and a Veil
sum: The chapter describes the tent itself. Ten curtains of fine linen woven with cherubim form the inner dwelling, joined by gold clasps into "one" (26:6). Over them hangs a tent of goat-hair cloth, and over that two coverings of leather. Gilded frames of acacia wood stand in silver bases and are held together by crossbars. A veil woven with cherubim divides the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark stands; in the outer room stand the table and lampstand, and a screen closes the entrance.

It is the most technical chapter in the Bible, and readers have drawn very different plans from it. Yet its point is simple: God's dwelling is a tent like Israel's tents, moving with them, and at its heart is a room no one may enter except as God allows.

views.H: A structure about 45 by 15 feet inside, built in the desert. Portable shrines of frames and curtains are known from Egypt, and the war camp of Ramesses II at Kadesh, about 1274 BC, had a royal tent with a similar two-room plan in a courtyard twice as long as it was wide.
views.M: The basic form of a curtained tent shrine may be old, while the gold, the silver bases and the precise symmetry may reflect later priestly elaboration.
views.C: Wellhausen called it the temple made portable, and many still see the tent as a priestly ideal modeled on Solomon's temple with its dimensions halved. Cross argued that it reflects David's tent for the ark, and Haran that it mirrors the Jerusalem temple's inner rooms. The proportions (a 10-cubit cube inside a 30-by-10-cubit tent) show a love of order more than a builder's practicality.
views.J: The Talmud (Shabbat 98b) and the Baraita of the Tabernacle debate the details: whether the frames were a cubit thick, how the curtains hung down the back. Rashi gives exact measurements. The veil became the model for the parokhet that hangs before the Torah ark in synagogues.
views.X: Hebrews 9:1–10 reads the two rooms as a lesson: while the outer room stood, the way into the holiest was not yet open. The torn temple veil at Jesus' death (Mark 15:38) and the "fresh, living road through the veil, which is his flesh" (Hebrews 10:20) make the veil one of the most-used tabernacle images in Christian preaching.

deep.b: Ancient and modern drawings disagree. The rabbis debated whether the frames were solid planks a cubit thick (Shabbat 98b) or slender; many modern scholars, following A. R. S. Kennedy, think they were open frames that let the cherub curtains show through (see 26:15). It is also unclear how the curtains hung: one view drapes the linen over the top and down the sides, outside the frames; another hangs it inside as a ceiling. Since the curtains measure 28 by 40 cubits and the frames enclose 10 by 30, neither reading fits every number perfectly. Richard Friedman proposed that the tabernacle was small enough to stand inside Solomon's temple, between the cherubim, though few have followed him.

The tent's walls used 48 frames, each 10 cubits high and 1.5 wide: 20 on the south, 20 on the north, and 8 on the west, including two corner frames (26:15–25). A cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, about 18 inches (45 cm), so the inner room was about 15 feet in each direction.

echoes: Exodus 36:8–38; Numbers 4:4–15; 2 Samuel 7:2–6; 1 Kings 6:14–36; Mark 15:38; Hebrews 6:19–20; Hebrews 9:1–10; Hebrews 10:19–22; Revelation 21:16

settings.what: Instructions for the dwelling
settings.to: Moses, for the craftsmen
settings.when: On the mountain
settings.why: To describe the tent itself. There are ten linen curtains woven with cherubim, a goat-hair tent over them, and leather coverings. Upright frames stand in silver bases, and a veil divides the holy place from the most holy place. The instructions bind the craftsmen to follow the plan exactly. They answer how a people on the move can carry God's house: it comes apart and goes with them.
settings.readers: For Israel the tent was a royal court in cloth. The cherubim woven into the curtains and the veil recalled the guarded garden of Eden (Genesis 3:24).

title: The Altar and the Courtyard
sum: Outside the tent stands the altar for burnt offerings: a hollow box of acacia wood covered with bronze, five cubits square, with horns at its corners, a bronze grating, and poles for carrying. Around everything runs a courtyard of linen hangings on bronze-based posts, a hundred cubits by fifty, with a colorful screen for a gate on the east. The chapter ends with the people bringing pure olive oil so that the lamp in the tent can burn from evening to morning.

The materials change as one moves outward, from gold inside to bronze outside, and the courtyard is the place where ordinary Israelites came with their gifts. The altar is where the people met God; the lamp is where the priests kept watch for him.

views.H: A real bronze-covered altar, light enough to carry. Critics ask how fire could burn in a wooden box; traditional answers are that it was filled with earth or stones (compare 20:24–25), as Rashi and others held.
views.M: Horned altars are well known from Israel and its neighbors, including the stone altar at Beersheba and the altar at Arad; the tradition of a portable altar may be early, with the bronze added in memory of Solomon's great altar.
views.C: Many critics note that the earthen or stone altar of 20:24–26 and this bronze altar come from different sources and periods, and that the courtyard mirrors the temple's courts. The lamp passage (27:20–21) interrupts and is often seen as a later addition, repeated in Leviticus 24:2–4.
views.J: The eternal light (ner tamid) in every synagogue recalls this lamp. The Talmud says the altar atones for Israel, and when the temple fell, the table in each home took its place (Berakhot 55a).
views.X: Hebrews 13:10 says "we have an altar" from which those who serve the tent may not eat, and Christian writers read the bronze altar as the cross, where the sacrifice was made before anyone could come nearer. The lamp burning all night became a picture of the church's prayer.

echoes: Exodus 20:24–26; Exodus 38:1–20; Leviticus 6:12–13; Leviticus 24:1–4; 1 Kings 1:50; 1 Kings 2:28; 1 Kings 8:64; Hebrews 13:10

settings.what: Instructions for the altar and the courtyard
settings.to: Moses, for the craftsmen
settings.when: On the mountain
settings.why: To describe the bronze altar for burnt offerings and the linen courtyard around the whole tent, with its gate on the east. The craftsmen build them. The priests serve at the altar, and ordinary Israelites may come into the court with their offerings, but not into the tent. The metals change from gold inside to bronze outside, showing the steps of holiness. The plan answers where the people may meet God: at the altar in the court.
settings.readers: For Israel the court was the place every worshiper could reach. The same plan of court, holy place and most holy place shaped the Temple.

settings.what: The law of the lamp oil
settings.to: Moses, to command the Israelites; and Aaron and his sons, who tend the lamp
settings.when: In the tent of meeting, through all generations
settings.why: To command the people to bring pure pressed olive oil, and the priests to keep the lamp burning from evening until morning before the LORD. It binds the whole people to supply it and the priests to serve, as a rule for all time. It answers how the people take part in the worship they may not enter: their oil keeps the light burning.
settings.readers: For Israel the lamp that always burned lives on in the eternal light of every synagogue.

title: Clothes for Honor and Beauty
sum: God chooses Aaron and his sons as priests and describes their holy clothes in detail. The high priest wears an ephod, a woven garment of gold, blue, purple and scarlet, with two onyx stones on its shoulders bearing the names of Israel's twelve tribes; a square breastpiece set with twelve engraved stones, holding the Urim and Thummim, so that Aaron carries Israel's names and decisions over his heart; a blue robe hemmed with pomegranates and gold bells; and a turban with a gold plate reading "Holy to the LORD." The ordinary priests receive tunics, sashes and headbands, and all wear linen underclothes.

The clothes are "for glory and for beauty" (28:2, 40). They make the priest a walking sanctuary in the same colors and materials as the tent, and they turn him into the people's representative: whenever he goes in before God, Israel goes in with him.
readings: Read as vestments

Read literally, the chapter describes what the priests wore, and Josephus, the Talmud and later Jewish tradition preserve detailed memories of the high priest's dress in the Second Temple. Ben Sira 50 describes Simon the high priest coming out in these clothes "like the morning star."
Read as symbols

Philo and Josephus read the clothes as a picture of the universe: the blue robe the air, the bells and pomegranates thunder and lightning, the twelve stones the zodiac. Christian readers saw a picture of Christ the high priest who carries his people's names on his heart (Hebrews 4:14–16).

views.H: Real garments made for Aaron. Gold thread, dyed wool and linen, and engraved gems were all available in the Late Bronze Age, and Egyptian priests also wore linen and pectorals.
views.M: The ephod, the Urim and Thummim and the bells may be old priestly items (the ephod and lots appear in early stories about David and Saul), gathered here into a single uniform for the high priest of later times.
views.C: A priestly ideal from the exile or after, when the high priest became the leading figure of the Jewish community and wore royal colors and a crown-like plate (compare Zechariah 3–6). The chapter gives priestly authority a Mosaic origin.
views.J: The weekly reading Tetzaveh is often said to be the one portion from Moses' birth to the end of Numbers in which his name does not appear; the Baal HaTurim and others connect this with his plea to be wiped from God's book (32:32). The Talmud says each garment atones for a sin (Zevachim 88b). The Yom Kippur liturgy recalls the high priest's appearance.
views.X: Hebrews calls Jesus "a great high priest" who sympathizes with weakness and enters the true sanctuary (4:14–16; 9:11–12). 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 1:6 call all believers priests, and the church borrowed from this chapter for its vestments, though Reformers objected to that.

deep.h: Names on the shoulders and over the heart
deep.b: The high priest carries Israel's names twice: on two onyx stones on his shoulders, six names each, "to bring them to mind" (28:12), and on twelve stones over his heart (28:29). The rabbis connected the shoulders with bearing burdens and the heart with love. The idea that a mediator holds a people's names before God, on his strength and on his affections, runs through the Bible, from the plea "Put me like a seal on your heart" (Song of Songs 8:6) to Jesus' prayer for "the ones you have given me" (John 17:9). The breastpiece is the means of "decisions" (mishpat): the priest carries both the people and the way to God's judgment for them (28:30).

deep.title: A priest dressed as a tabernacle
deep.body: My own reading, building on Haran and others: the high priest's clothes use the same materials and workmanship as the tent, gold and blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen, "the work of a skilled designer" (26:1, 31; 28:6, 15). The closer a piece of cloth is to the ark, the richer it is, and the high priest wears the richest of all. Dressed this way, he is the sanctuary on the move: the one part of the holy place that can go out to the people and come back in for them.

echoes: Exodus 39:1–31; Leviticus 8:7–9; Leviticus 16:4; 1 Samuel 2:18; 1 Samuel 14:41; 1 Samuel 23:9–12; Zechariah 3:3–5; Zechariah 14:20–21; Hebrews 4:14–16; 1 Peter 2:5–9; Revelation 1:13; Revelation 21:19–20

settings.what: Instructions for the priests' clothes
settings.to: Moses, about Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, and for the skilled workers who will make the clothes
settings.when: On the mountain
settings.why: To set apart Aaron's family as priests and to describe their holy clothes "for glory and for beauty." There is the ephod with the tribes' names on its shoulders, and the breastpiece with twelve stones and the Urim and Thummim. There is the blue robe with bells, and the gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD." The rules bind Aaron and his descendants whenever they serve. They answer how a sinful people can be represented before God. The high priest carries Israel's names over his heart and bears the guilt of their holy gifts (28:38).
settings.readers: For Israel the high priest's clothes showed the whole people carried into God's presence. Every tribe was named on his shoulders and over his heart.
views: Traditional readers see the priesthood given to Aaron's family at Sinai.
A Priestly source before the exile
Kaufmann, Haran and Milgrom date the Priestly source (P), and so this chapter, to the time of the First Temple.
Many other scholars think the chapter supports the Aaronic priests of Jerusalem in the late monarchy or after the exile.

traditions.q: Does the church have priests, as Israel had Aaron and his sons?
views: Yes. All the baptized share in Christ's priesthood, but the ordained priest differs in kind, not only in degree, and acts in the person of Christ at the altar (Catechism 1547, 1592). Bishops pass on Holy Orders in an unbroken line from the apostles.
Yes. Bishops, priests and deacons are ordained in apostolic succession, and the priest offers the Eucharist for the people. Orthodox vestments, like Aaron's, are worn for beauty and honor in worship.

All baptized Christians are priests (Luther, To the Christian Nobility, 1520). God has given an office of preaching and the sacraments, and only those rightly called should hold it (Augsburg Confession, articles 5 and 14), but its ministers do not offer sacrifice for sin.

Christ is the only priest, and his sacrifice ended the priesthood of Aaron (Hebrews 7:23–28). The church has ministers of the word, elders and deacons, and the Reformed removed priestly vestments in favor of a plain preaching gown.

The Anglican ordinal keeps bishops, priests and deacons. Anglicans are divided on what "priest" means: Anglo-Catholics hold a priesthood like the Catholic one, while evangelicals read it as "presbyter" or elder. In 1896 Pope Leo XIII declared Anglican orders invalid.

Every believer is a priest with direct access to God through Christ (1 Peter 2:9). The church's officers are pastors and deacons chosen by the congregation, and they are not priests (Baptist Faith and Message, article 6).

title: Seven Days of Ordination
sum: God gives the rite for making Aaron and his sons priests. They are washed, dressed and anointed with oil. A bull is offered as a sin offering, a ram as a burnt offering, and a second ram as the ram of ordination, whose blood is put on the priest's right ear, thumb and big toe and sprinkled with oil on their clothes. Portions are waved before the LORD and eaten by the priests in the holy place. The rite lasts seven days, and the altar itself is cleansed and made most holy.

The chapter ends with the daily offering of two lambs, morning and evening, and with God's purpose for the whole tabernacle: "I will live among the Israelites, and I will be their God," and they will know that he brought them out of Egypt for this (29:45–46). The exodus, it turns out, was so that God could live with his people.

views.H: The ordination took place as Leviticus 8–9 reports, with Moses acting as priest for the occasion. The closest known parallel is the installation of a high priestess of Baal at Emar in Syria (about 1200 BC), studied by Daniel Fleming, a rite of anointing, offerings and feasting that lasted nine days.
views.M: An old rite of ordination with blood and oil may lie behind the chapter, written up in the form later priests practiced.
views.C: P's ordination rite, carried out in Leviticus 8. It gives the Aaronite priesthood of the Second Temple a founding act at Sinai. The order of offerings (purification, burnt, then shared) reflects the developed sacrificial system of Leviticus 1–7.
views.J: The rabbis linked the daily offering (tamid) to the daily prayers, which replaced it after AD 70 (Berakhot 26b). The words "I will live among the Israelites" (29:45) are read as the goal of the whole Torah.
views.X: Hebrews contrasts priests who stand daily offering the same sacrifices (10:11) with Christ who offered one sacrifice for all time. The anointed priest points to the Messiah, the "anointed one," and the blood on ear, hand and foot was read by preachers as consecrating the whole person to hearing, doing and walking with God.

deep.b: Verse 46 gives a remarkable reason for the exodus: "to live in their midst." The book has said Israel was freed to worship (3:12; 7:16), to know the LORD (6:7), and to be his treasured people (19:5–6). Here the purpose is fulfilled on God's side: not only that Israel comes to God, but that God comes to Israel. Ramban made this the key to the book: the exile in Egypt ends not at the sea or at Sinai, but when the glory fills the tabernacle (40:34), and the people are back where the patriarchs stood, with God's presence among them.

echoes: Exodus 6:7; Exodus 25:8; Exodus 40:12–15; Leviticus 8:1–36; Leviticus 26:11–12; Numbers 28:3–8; Ezekiel 37:27; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Hebrews 7:27; Hebrews 10:11–14; Revelation 21:3

settings.what: The rite of ordination
settings.to: Moses, who is to perform it, for Aaron and his sons
settings.when: To be done once the tabernacle is built (Leviticus 8 tells how it was done)
settings.why: To give the seven-day rite that makes Aaron and his sons priests. They are washed, dressed and anointed. A bull is offered as a sin offering, a ram as a burnt offering, and the ram of ordination, whose blood is put on the right ear, thumb and big toe. The altar too is made most holy. The rite answers how ordinary men may serve the holy God: they must be cleansed, clothed and set apart.
settings.readers: For Israel the rite was the founding of its priesthood. Every later priest of Aaron's line stood in this ordination.

settings.what: The daily offering and God's purpose
settings.to: Moses, for the priests and all Israel
settings.when: For every day, through all generations
settings.why: To command two yearling lambs a day, morning and evening, at the entrance of the tent where God will meet Israel. It binds the priests to offer them and the people to supply them, every day for all time. Then comes the purpose of the whole plan: "I will live among the Israelites, and I will be their God" (29:45). They will know that he led them out of Egypt to live among them. The rule answers how God's presence is kept day after day.
settings.readers: For Israel the exodus itself was for this: God living among his people. The morning and evening offerings set the times of daily prayer.

title: Incense, Ransom, Water and Oil
sum: The chapter adds four items. The small gold altar of incense stands before the veil, and Aaron burns fragrant incense on it morning and evening; once a year its horns are cleansed with blood. When the people are counted, each man pays half a shekel as a ransom for his life, rich and poor the same, and the silver is used for the tent. A bronze basin stands between the tent and the altar for the priests to wash their hands and feet. Finally God gives the recipes for the holy anointing oil and the holy incense, which no one may copy for private use.

These instructions come after the priests and their clothes, not with the other furniture. Some readers see a deliberate order: once God has described how he will come to the people, he describes how they will come to him, with prayer, ransom, washing and anointing.

views.H: Real objects and rites given at Sinai. Small horned incense altars are well known from Israel, and four-ingredient incense blends fit what is known of ancient spices from Arabia and the Levant.
views.M: The incense altar may belong to a later stage of practice; incense altars are common in Iron Age Israel, and an incense burner may have been part of an older shrine.
views.C: Many critics since Wellhausen regard 30–31 as supplements to the original P instructions, since the incense altar is missing where it would be expected (26:35) and 29:42–46 sounds like an ending. The census tax reflects the Second Temple half-shekel (compare Nehemiah 10:32 and Matthew 17:24).
views.J: The half-shekel became the yearly temple tax, collected each spring (Mishnah Shekalim), and the reading of 30:11–16 (Parashat Shekalim) is still read on the Sabbath before the month of Adar. The Talmud lists eleven incense spices, and the passage on them (Pitum haketoret) is recited in daily prayer.
views.X: Christians connect incense with prayer (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4), the ransom money with Jesus' paying of the temple tax and his life given "as a ransom for many" (Matthew 17:24–27; Mark 10:45), and the basin with baptism and washing (Titus 3:5; Hebrews 10:22).

deep.b: The puzzle of the incense altar's placement is discussed at 26:35. The Samaritan Pentateuch and 4QpaleoExod-m move 30:1–10 there (see the variant at 26:35), and the Greek leaves out the making of this altar in chapter 37 (see 37:25). Cassuto answered that chapter 30 is about the service, not the structure: incense is what happens inside every day, and it belongs with the lamps Aaron tends at the same times (30:7–8).

echoes: Exodus 37:25–29; Exodus 38:8; Exodus 38:25–28; Leviticus 10:1–2; Leviticus 16:12–18; Numbers 1:1–3; Numbers 16:46–48; 2 Samuel 24:1–17; Psalm 133:2; Psalm 141:2; Matthew 17:24–27; Mark 10:45; Luke 1:8–11; Revelation 8:3–4

settings.what: Instructions for the incense altar
settings.to: Moses, for Aaron
settings.when: On the mountain, ending the first speech
settings.why: To place a small gold altar before the veil, where Aaron burns incense morning and evening. Once a year he makes atonement on its horns. No other incense or offering may be put on it. It binds Aaron and the high priests after him, every morning and evening and once a year on the Day of Atonement, in the holy place before the veil. It answers how the priest brings incense and atonement near God's throne without entering the most holy place.
settings.readers: For Israel the rising incense became a picture of prayer (Psalm 141:2).

settings.what: The law of the census ransom
settings.to: Moses, for every man twenty years old and up who is counted in a census
settings.when: Whenever the people are counted
settings.why: To require half a shekel from each person counted, rich and poor the same, as a ransom for his life so that no plague strikes them. The silver serves the tent of meeting. A census was dangerous in the ancient world (compare 2 Samuel 24), and texts from Mari also link counting with cleansing rites. The law answers that danger and makes everyone equal before God.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the root of the half-shekel Temple tax of later times (Mishnah Shekalim; Matthew 17:24).

settings.what: The law of the bronze basin
settings.to: Moses, for Aaron and his sons
settings.when: For all time, whenever they serve
settings.why: To have the priests wash their hands and feet before they enter the tent or approach the altar, "so that they will not die." It binds the priests forever. It answers the danger of bringing uncleanness into God's presence.
settings.readers: For Israel washing before worship became a lasting custom, and the Temple had its great bronze basin (1 Kings 7:23).

settings.what: The recipes for the anointing oil and the incense
settings.by: The LORD (the fourth and fifth speeches)
settings.to: Moses, for the priests and the perfumers, and every Israelite
settings.when: Through all generations
settings.why: To give the formulas for the holy anointing oil and the holy incense. No one may copy them for private use, on pain of being cut off from the people. The rule binds every Israelite. It answers the problem of holy things becoming common.
settings.readers: For Israel incense was a real part of worship in the land. Residue on one of the two altars at the Judahite shrine at Arad, from the 700s BC, contained frankincense.

title: The Artist and the Sabbath
sum: God names the builders: Bezalel of the tribe of Judah, whom he has filled with the Spirit of God and with skill in every craft, and Oholiab of the tribe of Dan, with all the skilled workers. Then comes the seventh and last speech: the Sabbath. It is a sign between God and Israel forever, a reminder that the LORD makes them holy, and a covenant grounded in creation, since in six days God made heaven and earth and on the seventh "he stopped and caught his breath" (31:17). Whoever works on it is to be put to death. Finally God gives Moses the two tablets of the testimony, written by his own finger.

Placed between the plans and the building, the Sabbath law makes a point the rabbis drew out at once: even the work of building God's house stops on the seventh day. Holy time is more sacred than holy space.

views.H: Bezalel and Oholiab were real craftsmen of the generation of the exodus. The Sabbath was given as a sign at Sinai, though already known from the manna (16:23–30).
views.M: The names may preserve real memories (Bezalel appears in Judah's genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2:20). The Sabbath is old in Israel, but its role as the defining covenant sign probably grew during the exile.
views.C: P's Sabbath theology, closely tied to the creation account of Genesis 1:1–2:3, which most critics also assign to P. In the exile, without land or temple, the Sabbath and circumcision became the marks of Jewish identity, and this passage gives the Sabbath covenant status.
views.J: The rabbis derived the 39 categories of forbidden Sabbath work from the crafts used to build the tabernacle, because the Sabbath law is placed here (Shabbat 49b). Verses 16–17, Veshamru, are sung in the Friday evening and Sabbath morning prayers. The Talmud says Bezalel "knew how to combine the letters by which heaven and earth were created" (Berakhot 55a).
views.X: Christian writers have pointed to Bezalel to honor artistic gifts as gifts of the Spirit. Most Christians keep Sunday, the day of resurrection, and read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ's rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), while Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep the seventh day.

deep.b: The Sabbath is the subject of the seventh speech that began at 25:1, and it shares key words with Genesis 2:1–3: "the seventh day," "work," "made," "heavens and earth," "holy." Read with the creation account, the instructions for the tabernacle become a second creation that ends, as the first did, with God's rest. When the building begins, Moses repeats the Sabbath first (35:1–3), so the Sabbath frames the whole calf story in between.

echoes: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 2:1–3; Exodus 16:23–30; Exodus 20:8–11; Exodus 35:1–3; Exodus 35:30–36:2; Numbers 15:32–36; Deuteronomy 5:12–15; Deuteronomy 9:10; Isaiah 56:2–7; Ezekiel 20:12; Mark 2:27; Luke 11:20; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Hebrews 4:9–10

settings.what: The call of Bezalel and Oholiab
settings.to: Moses, about the craftsmen
settings.when: On the mountain
settings.why: To name Bezalel of the tribe of Judah, filled with the Spirit of God and with skill in every craft. With him come Oholiab of the tribe of Dan and all the skilled workers, to make everything. It answers who can build what God has shown: only those whom God himself gifts. Bezalel is the first person the Bible calls filled with the Spirit of God, and the gift is for art.
settings.readers: For Israel this honored craft as holy work. One master came from the leading tribe and one from a small tribe of the far north, so the whole people shared in the building.

settings.what: The Sabbath sign
settings.to: Moses, to tell the Israelites
settings.when: At the end of the tabernacle instructions
settings.why: To command the Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel forever, that the LORD makes them holy, with death for anyone who works on it. As God made the world in six days and rested, so the builders of his dwelling must rest. The seven speeches end like the seven days of creation. It binds every Israelite through all generations, even during holy work.
settings.readers: For Israel the Sabbath was its mark among the nations. In exile, without a temple, the Sabbath became Israel's sanctuary in time.
views: Peter Kearney traced the seven speeches to the seven days of creation, and Moshe Weinfeld linked Sabbath, temple and God's enthronement.
Many critical scholars see the stress on the Sabbath as a sign for Jews living among the nations after 586 BC.

title: The Golden Calf
sum: While Moses is on the mountain, the people grow afraid that he is gone for good and press Aaron to make them gods to lead them. He collects their gold earrings and makes a calf, and they say, "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" Aaron builds an altar and declares a festival for the LORD. On the mountain God tells Moses and threatens to wipe the people out and make a nation of Moses instead. Moses pleads, and God relents. Coming down, Moses sees the dancing, smashes the tablets, burns and grinds the calf, and makes the people drink it.

Aaron blames the people and the fire. Moses calls, "Whoever is on the LORD's side, to me!" and the Levites rally to him and kill three thousand. Moses goes back up and offers to be wiped out of God's book if God will not forgive. God refuses the offer, promises an angel to lead them, and sends a plague. The covenant just made at Sinai is broken almost before the ink is dry.
readings: Read as apostasy

The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: at the foot of the mountain where they heard "You must have no other gods," the people worship an idol. The calf is Israel's original sin, the pattern for every later unfaithfulness.
Read as forbidden worship of the LORD

Many scholars, ancient and modern, notice that Aaron proclaims "a festival for the LORD" (32:5) and the people credit the calf with the exodus. On this reading the calf was meant as a pedestal or image of Israel's own God, like the cherubim, and the sin was breaking the second commandment (no images) more than the first.
Read as a story against Bethel

Critical scholars point to 1 Kings 12:28, where Jeroboam sets up two calves with nearly the same words, "Here are your gods, Israel." They read the Exodus story as told, or retold, in Judah to condemn the northern shrines at Bethel and Dan, perhaps with a dig at priests there who claimed descent from Aaron.

views.H: The event happened as told at Sinai. Bull imagery was common in Egypt (the Apis bull) and Canaan (Baal and El were called "bull"), so a people fresh from Egypt could easily have made one.
views.M: A real memory of calf worship at an early shrine may lie behind the story, retold later to explain why God's presence is invisible and to condemn the northern calves.
views.C: Mostly from the non-priestly sources, heavily edited, with layers: the intercession (32:7–14), the Levites' slaughter (32:25–29) and the plague (32:35) are three different punishments. The story was probably shaped after Jeroboam's calves (late 900s BC) and reworked in Deuteronomistic language (compare Deuteronomy 9:7–21). Several recent scholars, Dozeman among them, go further and treat much of 32–34 as written after Deuteronomy, or even after the priestly source, as a bridge between the two.
views.J: The Talmud says every later punishment holds a share of the calf (Sanhedrin 102a). Midrash blames the mixed crowd from Egypt (12:38), defends Aaron as a man stalling for time after the people killed Hur (Sanhedrin 7a), and praises the women, who would not give their earrings (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 45). The fast of the 17th of Tammuz recalls the breaking of the tablets (Mishnah Taanit 4:6).
views.X: Stephen cites the calf as Israel's turning back to Egypt in their hearts (Acts 7:39–41); Paul quotes 32:6 to warn the Corinthians against idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:7). Christian theology reads Moses' offer to die for the people as a foreshadowing of Christ, who did die for them.

deep.b: The links between Exodus 32 and 1 Kings 12:26–33 are close. Both make gold calves; both say nearly the same words, "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt" (in Kings, "Here are your gods"), a plural strange for one calf in Exodus but natural for Jeroboam's two; both build an altar and hold a feast. Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu (24:1) and Jeroboam's sons Nadab and Abijah (1 Kings 14:1, 20) even share names, and both pairs die. Traditional readers see Jeroboam deliberately reviving Aaron's sin, and the writer of Kings telling it that way. Many critical scholars think the influence ran the other way: the Exodus story was written to say that the northern kingdom's worship had been a sin since Sinai. Some think Bethel's priests claimed Aaron as their ancestor, and that his calf was once told as legitimate.

The text says the LORD "relented" (nicham) about the harm he had planned (32:14). Elsewhere the Bible says God "is not a human being who changes his mind" (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Jewish and Christian theologians have answered in several ways: that God's threats are conditional, like Jonah's warning to Nineveh (Jeremiah 18:7–10); that God's eternal will includes his response to prayer; that the language describes God as he appears to us (Maimonides, Calvin); or, in open theism and some Jewish thinkers such as Abraham Joshua Heschel, that God truly responds and is moved. The story presents Moses' prayer as making a real difference.

deep.title: Aaron did what the people asked; Moses did what God did not ask
deep.body: My own observation: the chapter contrasts two mediators. Aaron gives the people what they demand, and then hides behind them ("You yourself know the people, how bent on evil they are," 32:22). Moses refuses what God offers him, a nation of his own (32:10), and then stands with the people against God's anger, even to the point of asking to be wiped out with them (32:32). A good mediator, the story suggests, does not simply pass along what either side wants.

echoes: Exodus 20:3–6; Exodus 24:1–8; Deuteronomy 9:7–21; 1 Kings 12:26–33; 1 Kings 14:9; Nehemiah 9:18; Psalm 106:19–23; Hosea 8:4–6; Hosea 13:2; Acts 7:39–41; Romans 9:3; 1 Corinthians 10:7

settings.what: The demand for gods and Aaron's festival
settings.to: Aaron; then the people
settings.when: When Moses is long delayed on the mountain
settings.why: The people ask Aaron to make gods to go before them, since Moses is gone. Aaron collects their gold, makes a calf, and proclaims a festival for the LORD. The people hail it as the gods who brought Israel up from Egypt. Weeks after the covenant, they break its second word.
settings.readers: For Israel the words were almost those of King Jeroboam at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28). So many scholars think Judah heard the story as a judgment on the northern calf shrines.
views: Traditional readers take it as Israel's first great sin, right after the covenant.
Many critical scholars think the story was shaped to condemn the calves of the northern kingdom.

Some think the calf, like the cherubim, was meant as a stand for the unseen LORD, which still broke the second word. A bronze bull from a hilltop shrine of the 1100s BC in the hills of Manasseh shows that such images were known in early Israel.

settings.what: Moses pleads for the people
settings.to: Moses on the mountain; then the LORD
settings.when: While the people celebrate below
settings.why: God tells Moses that the people have ruined themselves. He threatens to finish them off and make a great nation of Moses instead. Moses pleads: what will the Egyptians say, and remember your oath to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. The LORD relents. Moses refuses to become a new Abraham and stakes everything on God's promise and name.
settings.readers: For Israel this became the great model of a prophet standing in the gap (Psalm 106:23; Jeremiah 15:1).

settings.what: Joshua's report and Moses' answer
settings.to: Moses; then Joshua
settings.when: As they come down the mountain with the tablets
settings.why: Joshua hears the noise and thinks there is war in the camp. Moses answers in a short poem: it is not the sound of victory or of defeat, but the sound of singing. Moses already knows what God has told him.
settings.readers: For Israel the poem turned a victory cry into a judgment. The people who sang at the sea (15:1) now sing to a calf.

settings.what: Aaron's excuse
settings.to: Moses
settings.when: When Moses comes down and destroys the calf
settings.why: To shift the blame: the people are bent on evil, and the calf simply came out of the fire. The lame excuse shows how leaders dodge guilt.
settings.readers: For Israel the excuse echoed Adam blaming Eve in the garden (Genesis 3:12). Even its first high priest failed.

settings.what: The call to the Levites
settings.to: The Levites, who rally to him at the gate of the camp
settings.when: After the people have run wild
settings.why: To command them in the LORD's name to go through the camp with swords and kill, even brother and friend. About three thousand die. Moses says they have filled their hands for the LORD that day, an ordination.
settings.readers: For Israel the story explained the Levites' holy role (Deuteronomy 33:8–11). Its violence troubles many modern readers.

settings.what: Moses offers himself
settings.to: The people; then the LORD
settings.when: The next day
settings.why: Moses tells the people they have sinned greatly and goes up to make atonement. He asks God to forgive them, or else to wipe him out of his book. God answers that he will wipe out only the one who sinned. He sends Moses on with an angel, though a day of reckoning will come.
settings.readers: For Israel Moses was the leader who would give himself for the people. Paul echoes his offer in Romans 9:3.

title: Show Me Your Glory
sum: God tells Moses to lead the people on to the promised land, with an angel going ahead, but says he himself will not go with them, or he might destroy them on the way. The people mourn and strip off their ornaments. The narrator then describes how Moses used to pitch a tent of meeting outside the camp, where the pillar of cloud came down and the LORD spoke with Moses "face to face." Moses pleads again: "If your face is not going, do not bring us up from here." God agrees.

Then Moses asks for more: "Please let me see your glory." God promises to make his goodness pass by and to call out his name, but warns that no one can see his face and live. He will set Moses in a crack in the rock, cover him with his hand, and let him see his back. The chapter is the Bible's deepest reflection on how near a person can come to God.
readings: Read as a vision

Read literally, Moses had a real experience of God's presence on the mountain, and the bodily language (face, hand, back) is the closest human words can come to it. Jewish and Christian mystics have treated this as the model of the soul's encounter with God.
Read as theology

Read as a reflection, the chapter balances two truths: God is near enough to speak with "face to face," yet too holy to be seen. Maimonides took "face" as God's essence and "back" as his works and ways, which can be known; Gregory of Nyssa took seeing God's back as following him.

views.H: Moses had both regular meetings with God in the tent and a single overwhelming vision on the mountain. The tent outside the camp was an interim meeting place before the tabernacle was built.
views.M: The tent outside the camp may preserve an old tradition of a simple tent shrine where a prophet received oracles, different from the later priestly picture of the tabernacle in the camp's center.
views.C: A collection of non-priestly units, each answering the question raised by the calf: will God still go with Israel? The tent of meeting outside the camp (33:7–11, an E tradition) clashes with P's tabernacle in the center. The vision passage reworks older material into a theology of God's name.
views.J: The rabbis said Moses saw "the knot of God's tefillin" at the back of his head (Berakhot 7a). Rashi reads 33:11 as Moses returning to the camp to teach the people. The words "I will show grace to whoever I show grace" became central to Jewish ideas of grace, and the cleft of the rock appears in the hymns of Yom Kippur.
views.X: John 1:14–18 alludes to this chapter: "We gazed at his glory... full of grace and truth... Nobody has ever seen God. It is the only one, God, the one in the Father's embrace, who has made him known." Paul quotes 33:19 to argue that God's mercy is free (Romans 9:15). The hymn "Rock of Ages, cleft for me" draws on 33:22.

deep.h: Face to face, but not the face
deep.b: The chapter seems to contradict itself: God speaks with Moses "face to face" (33:11), then says "You cannot see my face" (33:20). Most interpreters read "face to face" as an idiom for direct, friendly speech, as Numbers 12:8 says God spoke to Moses "mouth to mouth," while seeing God's face means seeing him as he is. Critical scholars add that the two passages come from different sources. Readers have also noticed that "face" (panim) is the key word of the chapter: God's face will go with them (33:14–15), the people stand at their tent doors facing the tent (33:10), and Moses may not see God's face (33:20, 23). The question of the chapter is whether God's presence, his face, will go with Israel. The answer is yes, but not as something to look at.

deep.h: Rashi, Ramban and the order of the story
deep.b: Rashi held that the tabernacle commands were given after the calf, as a sign of forgiveness, and Ramban that they were God's plan from the start, a portable Sinai (see the note on 31:18). Either way, many modern readers see the order of the book as deliberate: the plan, the sin, and then the rebuilding.

deep.title: The tent pitched far off
deep.body: My own reading: in 33:7 Moses pitches the tent "outside the camp, at a distance from the camp," just after God says he will not go "in among" the people (33:3, 5). The tent's distance acts out God's words. By 40:34–38 the glory fills the tabernacle at the center of the camp. The book's last chapters, read this way, are the story of a distance closed: God moving from outside the camp back into its middle.

echoes: Genesis 32:30; Exodus 3:6; Exodus 24:9–11; Numbers 12:8; Numbers 14:14; Deuteronomy 34:10; 1 Kings 19:9–13; Isaiah 6:1–5; Matthew 5:8; John 1:14–18; Romans 9:15; 2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 Timothy 6:16; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4

settings.what: God's refusal to go up in their midst
settings.to: Moses, to tell the Israelites
settings.when: After the plague
settings.why: To send them on to the land with an angel, but to refuse to go in their midst. They are a stiff-necked people, and he might finish them off on the way. The people mourn and strip off their ornaments.
settings.readers: For Israel the words raised the crisis the tabernacle was meant to solve: can a holy God live among a sinful people?

settings.what: Moses asks to see God's glory
settings.to: Each other, in the tent of meeting and at the mountain
settings.when: After the people mourn
settings.why: Moses asks to know God's ways and pleads that God's own face go with them, and God agrees. Then Moses asks to see God's glory. God will make his goodness pass by and call out his name, and show grace to whom he chooses. But no one can see his face and live, so Moses will see his back from a cleft in the rock.
settings.readers: For Israel the scene taught that God's presence is a gift of grace. He is known by his name and goodness, not by his face.

title: The LORD, the LORD
sum: God tells Moses to cut two new stone tablets and come up the mountain alone. The LORD comes down in the cloud and passes in front of him, calling out his name: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness, forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin, yet by no means leaving guilt unpunished. Moses bows and asks God to go with this stubborn people and take them as his own. God answers by making a covenant, with a list of commands: no covenants with the peoples of the land, no other gods and no metal images, the festivals, the firstborn, the Sabbath, and the first fruits.

Moses stays forty days and nights without food and writes "the Ten Words" on the tablets. When he comes down, the skin of his face is shining, and the people are afraid. From then on he covers his face with a veil, except when he speaks with God or passes God's words on.

views.H: The covenant renewal and the shining face happened as told. The commands of 34:11–26 are a summary of the covenant terms most relevant after the calf: worship and festivals.
views.M: The chapter may preserve an old covenant ceremony at a mountain shrine, and an early list of festival laws.
views.C: Wellhausen and others called 34:14–26 the "ritual decalogue," an older version of the covenant laws than chapter 20 (Goethe had already argued this in 1773). The parallels with 23:12–19 are close. The shining face story may draw on priestly or prophetic masks, or explain why Moses was pictured veiled.
views.J: The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy (34:6–7) are recited on fast days, at the Selichot prayers, before the open ark on festivals, and throughout Yom Kippur. The Talmud says God himself showed Moses how to pray them, wrapped like a prayer leader (Rosh Hashanah 17b). The rabbis held that Moses came down with the second tablets on Yom Kippur.
views.X: John 1:14–17 ("full of grace and truth") echoes "great in loyal love and faithfulness." Paul contrasts Moses' veiled face with the unveiled faces of believers who reflect the Lord's glory (2 Corinthians 3:7–18). Jerome's Latin, "his face was horned," gave Western art its horned Moses.

deep.b: Moses asked to see God's glory and received God's name. The words of 34:6–7 are repeated or echoed more than any other description of God in the Hebrew Bible: by Moses (Numbers 14:18), in the Psalms (86:15; 103:8; 145:8), by Joel (2:13), Jonah (4:2), Nahum (1:3) and Nehemiah (9:17). Most quote only the merciful half. Jonah quotes it as a complaint: he fled because he knew God would forgive Nineveh. Nahum quotes the other half, "he will by no means leave guilt unpunished," against the same city. The passage holds mercy and justice together, but the proportion is unequal: love "to thousands" against consequences for "the third and the fourth generation."

The verb qaran in 34:29 comes from qeren, "horn," and can mean "send out rays." Aquila's Greek and Jerome's Latin Vulgate both took it as "horned" (cornuta), and Jerome seems to have meant it as a sign of glory, since horns stood for power. From the eleventh century Western artists gave Moses horns, most famously Michelangelo's statue in Rome (1515). Ruth Mellinkoff showed that the horns began as a mark of honor; only later did they merge with the slander that Jews had horns. Other readings of the verb are given in the note on 34:29. Most translations since the Reformation render the verb "shone."

deep.title: Glory asked for, goodness given
deep.body: My own observation: Moses asks to see God's "glory" (33:18), and God answers that he will show his "goodness" and his "name" (33:19), and then proclaims his character (34:6–7). The glory that Moses could not see turns out to be a set of moral qualities he can hear. The chapter ends with Moses' face reflecting a glory he did not know he carried (34:29). Exodus seems to teach that one sees God's glory not by looking at it but by being changed by his words.

echoes: Exodus 20:1–17; Exodus 20:5–6; Exodus 23:12–19; Numbers 14:18; Deuteronomy 7:9–10; Deuteronomy 10:1–5; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 86:15; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nahum 1:3; John 1:14–17; 2 Corinthians 3:7–18

settings.what: The name of the LORD proclaimed, and Moses' plea
settings.by: The LORD, passing in front of Moses; then Moses
settings.to: Moses, standing on the rock; then the Lord
settings.when: On the mountain, in the morning
settings.why: The LORD proclaims his own character: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness." He forgives guilt, rebellion and sin, yet does not leave guilt unpunished. After the calf, this is the answer to whether God can still live with Israel. Moses bows and asks the Lord to go in their midst, stiff-necked as they are, and to forgive them. The very reason God gave for not going (33:3) becomes Moses' reason for asking him to go.
settings.readers: For Israel these words became a creed, repeated again and again (Numbers 14:18; Psalm 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). Jews recite them as the thirteen attributes of mercy on fast days and the High Holy Days.

settings.what: The covenant renewed
settings.to: Moses, for Israel
settings.when: On the mountain, with the new tablets
settings.why: To renew the covenant with promised wonders and a short list of commands. Make no covenant with the peoples of the land, and tear down their altars and sacred poles. Make no cast gods, and keep the three feasts. Give the firstborn and the first fruits. Rest on the seventh day, even at plowing and harvest. Do not boil a young goat in its mother's milk. It binds Israel above all as it enters the land and meets its peoples and gods. The list answers the sin of the calf by stressing worship of the LORD alone.
settings.readers: For Israel the list repeated much of 23:12–19. Its stress on worship spoke to a people always tempted by the gods of the land.
views: Goethe, and many scholars since, saw here a second set of ten commands, mostly about worship.
Traditional readers take it as the main terms of the covenant restated after the calf, with the tablets still bearing the Ten Words of chapter 20 (34:28).

settings.what: The command to write the covenant
settings.to: Moses, after forty days on the mountain
settings.when: At the end of the covenant renewal
settings.why: To tell Moses to write these words down, because on them God has made a covenant with him and with Israel. Moses stays forty days and nights without bread or water, and the Ten Words are written on the tablets. The broken covenant is now a written text again.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the root of its book of the covenant. The tradition that Moses wrote down God's words begins in verses like this one.

title: Everyone Whose Heart Was Willing
sum: Moses gathers the whole community. He begins with the Sabbath: six days of work, a seventh day of complete rest, and no fire lit in their homes. Then he asks for the offering God described in chapter 25, and for skilled people to make everything. Men and women come, "every person whose heart lifted him," bringing jewelry, yarn, skins, wood, oil, spices and stones. Skilled women spin blue, purple and scarlet yarn and goat hair. Moses announces that God has chosen Bezalel and Oholiab, filled them with skill, and given them the ability to teach.

With this chapter the second half of the tabernacle story begins. Most of chapters 35–40 repeats the instructions of 25–31 almost word for word, now as things done. After the calf, the repetition itself is the message: the people are doing exactly what God asked.

views.H: The building happened as reported. The repetition reflects ancient building accounts, which often recorded both the order and its execution (as in the Mesopotamian and Ugaritic texts studied by Victor Hurowitz).
views.M: The account may expand a shorter tradition about a tent shrine into a full parallel of the commands.
views.C: Part of P, but often thought to be a later layer than 25–31, since the Greek text of 35–40 differs so much (see 36:8). The repetition fills out the commands in narrative form, possibly by a later editor.
views.J: This begins the reading Vayaqhel ("he assembled"), often read together with Pequdei. The Talmud derived from 35:1–3 that the 39 kinds of work used in building the tabernacle are forbidden on the Sabbath (Shabbat 49b, 70a). The Karaites read the ban on fire as forbidding any light on the Sabbath; the Rabbanites lit lamps before it began.
views.X: Paul's appeal for generous, willing giving (2 Corinthians 8–9) draws on the spirit of this chapter, and preachers have often used the women's spinning and the willing gifts as models of service in the church.

deep.b: Chapters 35–40 repeat much of 25–31, in a new order (the tent before the ark) and in the past tense. Modern readers often find this tedious; ancient readers did not. Hurowitz showed that Near Eastern building inscriptions regularly repeated the god's command and the king's fulfillment. The repetition also proves a point: after the calf, Israel follows the instructions exactly. The refrain "as the LORD commanded Moses" appears seven times in chapter 39 and seven in chapter 40.

echoes: Exodus 25:1–9; Exodus 31:1–17; Exodus 32:2–3; Numbers 7:1–89; 1 Chronicles 29:1–9; Ezra 2:68–69; 2 Corinthians 8:1–15; 2 Corinthians 9:7

settings.what: The Sabbath first
settings.to: The whole community of the Israelites, gathered together
settings.when: When he comes down with the new tablets and the building is about to begin
settings.why: To repeat the Sabbath command before any work starts: six days of work, a seventh of complete rest, and no fire lit in their homes. It binds every household in the camp. Building God's house does not override God's day.
settings.readers: For Israel the link between the Sabbath and the tabernacle shaped its law. The Mishnah lists thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work (Shabbat 7:2), and the Talmud derives them from the work on the tabernacle (Shabbat 49b).

settings.what: The call for gifts and workers
settings.to: The whole community of the Israelites
settings.when: After the Sabbath command
settings.why: To pass on God's request of chapter 25: a gift from every willing heart, and every skilled person to come and make what the LORD commanded. Men and women alike respond.
settings.readers: For Israel the giving undid the calf. Once they gave their gold for an idol; now they gave it for God's dwelling.

title: More Than Enough
sum: The work begins. Bezalel, Oholiab and the skilled workers receive the gifts, but the people keep bringing more every morning, until the craftsmen tell Moses, "The people are bringing too much." Moses sends word through the camp to stop. Then the craftsmen make the tent: the linen curtains with cherubim and gold clasps, the goat-hair tent with bronze clasps, the leather coverings, the frames and bases and crossbars, the veil, and the entrance screen. Almost every verse repeats chapter 26.
This is the only place in the Bible where people are told to stop giving. The details of the building that follow differ most from the Greek text here (see the variant at 36:8).

views.H: The repetition records the actual building, which matched the plan. The generosity reflects the wealth taken from Egypt (12:35–36).
views.C: The repeated building account is often seen as a late supplement to P, and its different form in the Greek may preserve an earlier stage (see 36:8). The surplus of gifts contrasts deliberately with the calf (32:2–3).
views.J: The midrash says the leaders of the tribes held back, planning to give what was missing at the end, and were too late; so they brought the stones for the ephod instead, and the word for "leaders" is spelled short in 35:27 as a rebuke (Rashi on 35:27).
views.X: Preachers have often contrasted this willing surplus with Ananias and Sapphira, who held back (Acts 5:1–11), and with Paul's teaching that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).

settings.what: The order to stop giving
settings.to: Moses; then the whole camp, by a proclamation
settings.when: While the work is under way
settings.why: The craftsmen report that the people are bringing too much. Moses has it called out through the camp that no one should bring any more. The order answers a happy problem: the work has more than it needs.
settings.readers: For Israel it showed a people restored after the calf. It is the only time in the Bible that a leader has to stop people from giving.

title: Ark, Table, Lampstand and Incense
sum: Bezalel makes the furnishings: the ark of acacia wood covered with gold, its atonement lid with two cherubim facing each other, the table and its dishes, the lampstand hammered from a talent of pure gold with its almond-blossom cups, and the altar of incense with its horns and poles. Finally he makes the holy anointing oil and the pure fragrant incense. The chapter follows chapters 25 and 30 closely.
The narrator names Bezalel as the maker of the ark itself (37:1), a sign of his special honor. In the Greek the making of the incense altar is missing (see the variant at 37:25).

views.H: The furnishings were made as commanded. The detailed match between plan and work shows exact obedience.
views.C: Critics note that the anointing oil and incense are mentioned only in one verse (37:29), while their recipes in chapter 30 are long, and see this as a sign that 30:22–38 and the matching verses were added later.
views.J: The rabbis noticed that the furnishings described here were later made again for Solomon's temple, except the ark, which was never remade; the Mishnah says that in the Second Temple the most holy place was empty, with only a stone where the ark had stood (Mishnah Yoma 5:2).
views.X: Bede's On the Tabernacle reads the ark as Christ, his wood the incorruptible humanity and his gold the divinity; this reading was standard in medieval commentary.

title: Bronze, Mirrors and an Account
sum: Bezalel makes the bronze altar for burnt offerings and the bronze basin, made from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting. He sets up the courtyard of linen hangings on bronze posts with its colorful gate. Then comes an account of the materials, kept by the Levites under Ithamar son of Aaron: about a ton of gold, about three and a half tons of silver from the census money, and about two and a half tons of bronze, with exactly how each was used.
The account is the Bible's first audit. Every shekel of the people's gifts is traced to what it became, a sign that the holy work was done honestly.

views.H: A real account. The figures fit the amounts needed for the items described, and the silver total follows exactly from the census of 603,550 men in Numbers 1:46.
views.M: The totals may be idealized but are based on the structure's needs; ancient temple records also listed metals by weight.
views.C: The account presupposes the census of Numbers 1, which in the story has not yet happened (Numbers 1:1 dates it a month after the tabernacle was raised), suggesting that the passage was written with the whole priestly narrative in view.
views.J: The midrash says Moses refused the women's mirrors at first because they were tools of vanity, but God told him to accept them, because the women had used them in Egypt to win their weary husbands and keep Israel alive (Tanhuma, cited by Rashi on 38:8). Onkelos says the women "came to pray."
views.X: Paul's care to handle the collection for Jerusalem openly, "so that no one could find fault with us" (2 Corinthians 8:20–21), follows the same spirit of accountability.

deep.b: The silver adds up. 603,550 men paying half a shekel each gives 301,775 shekels. At 3,000 shekels to a talent, that is 100 talents and 1,775 shekels, exactly the figures in 38:25. A hundred talents went into the hundred bases (38:27), and the rest into hooks and bands for the posts (38:28). A shekel weighed about 11.4 grams (0.4 oz), so the silver came to about 3.4 metric tons.

title: As the LORD Commanded Moses
sum: The craftsmen make the priestly clothes: the ephod with its two onyx stones, the breastpiece with twelve stones in four rows, the blue robe with its pomegranates and bells, the tunics, turbans and sashes, and the gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD." Seven times the chapter says it was done "as the LORD commanded Moses." Then the people bring everything to Moses, piece by piece. He inspects it all, sees that they have done exactly what God commanded, and blesses them.

The chapter ends with echoes of the end of creation: the work "was finished" (39:32), Moses "saw all the work, and there it was: they had done it" (39:43), and he blesses them, as God looked at all he had made and blessed the seventh day (Genesis 1:31; 2:3).

views.H: The clothes were made as commanded. The inspection and blessing record the completion of the work, about nine months after the arrival at Sinai.
views.C: The sevenfold refrain is a priestly device, as in Genesis 1, and the inspection scene ties the tabernacle to creation. The Greek text has the clothes first, before the tent, and in a shorter form (see 36:8).
views.J: Rashi, following the midrash, says the craftsmen could not raise the tabernacle and brought it to Moses, who had done none of the work himself, and that God let him raise it (on 39:33). Rashi also says Moses' blessing was Psalm 90:17 (on 39:43), "make the work of our hands last," since Psalm 90 is titled "a prayer of Moses."
views.X: Christian writers have read the completed priestly clothes as the righteousness of Christ that clothes believers (Isaiah 61:10; Galatians 3:27), and the refrain of obedience as a picture of Jesus who did "everything the Father commanded" (John 14:31).

deep.b: The phrase "as the LORD commanded Moses" comes seven times in chapter 39 (39:1, 5, 7, 21, 26, 29, 31) and seven times in chapter 40 (40:19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 32). Genesis 1 uses its refrains ("and it was so," "God saw that it was good") in sevens too. The repetition answers the calf: there the people did what they wanted and Aaron made what they asked; here every piece is made as God asked. Sarna, Blenkinsopp and others see this as the key to the closing chapters: obedience completes what sin had broken.

deep.title: Moses blesses, as God blessed
deep.body: My own reading: in Genesis 1 God made, looked and blessed; in Exodus 39 the people make, Moses looks and Moses blesses. The roles have shifted. Human beings now do the making, under God's command, and the one who blesses is a man who has spoken with God. The tabernacle chapters may be telling us that the image of God from Genesis 1:26–27 is lived out not in ruling only but in making and blessing. The link between making and the image of God has also been drawn by Blenkinsopp, Fretheim and J. Richard Middleton; what I add is only the shift of roles in this one scene.

echoes: Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:1–3; Exodus 28:1–43; Leviticus 8:7–9; Numbers 7:1; Psalm 90:17; Isaiah 61:10; John 17:4

title: The Glory Fills the Tabernacle
sum: God tells Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month, a year after the exodus. Moses raises the frames, hangs the curtains, puts the tablets in the ark and the ark in the most holy place, sets the table, lampstand, incense altar, bronze altar and basin in their places, and hangs the screens, each time "as the LORD commanded Moses." He anoints everything and washes, dresses and anoints Aaron and his sons. "So Moses finished the work."

Then the cloud covers the tent and the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle, so that even Moses cannot go in. From then on, whenever the cloud lifts, Israel sets out, and when it stays, they stay, with the cloud by day and fire by night over the tabernacle, in sight of all Israel, through all their journeys. The book that began with Israel in slavery in Egypt ends with God living in their midst.
readings: Read as the goal of the exodus

On this reading, the book has been heading here from the start: God brought Israel out of Egypt "to live in their midst" (29:46). Ramban held that the exile ended not at the sea but when the glory came to rest in the tabernacle.
Read as a new creation

On this reading, the dedication on New Year's Day (40:2), the closing words "Moses finished the work" (40:33, compare Genesis 2:2), and God's glory settling in his house complete the second creation that began with the seven speeches of chapters 25–31. The world began with God's Spirit over the waters; the tabernacle begins with his glory over the tent.

views.H: The tabernacle was raised on the date given, and the cloud and fire were a visible miracle that guided Israel for forty years (Numbers 9:15–23).
views.M: A memory of a tent shrine that traveled with a group in the wilderness may lie behind the story, with the cloud as a theological description of God's guidance.
views.C: The climax of P's account and of Exodus as edited. Its goal is not history but theology: God's presence is with Israel wherever they are, which spoke powerfully to exiles without a temple. The scene parallels the dedication of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10–11) and Ezekiel's vision of the glory returning (Ezekiel 43:1–5).
views.J: The reading Pequdei ends the book, and the congregation rises and says, "Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened" (Chazak chazak venitchazek). The word shakhan, "settle" (40:35), gives the rabbinic term Shekhinah for God's dwelling presence. The Talmud says the day the sanctuary was dedicated brought God joy like the day heaven and earth were made (Megillah 10b).
views.X: John 1:14 ("the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us. We gazed at his glory") echoes 40:34–35. Christians read the filling of the tabernacle as fulfilled in Christ and in the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost, when the believers became God's temple (Acts 2:1–4; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Revelation 21:3).

deep.h: An ending that is also a beginning
deep.b: Exodus ends with Moses outside the tent, unable to enter (40:35). Leviticus begins with God calling to him from inside it (Leviticus 1:1). The rest of the Pentateuch tells how the people live with a holy God in their midst: what offerings to bring, how to stay pure, how to march with the tabernacle in the center (Numbers 2). The last verses look ahead to the whole wilderness journey (40:36–38), so the book closes with Israel ready to move, led by God's presence.

deep.title: From Egypt's buildings to God's
deep.body: My own observation: Exodus begins with Israel forced to build store cities for Pharaoh, "with hard labor in clay and bricks" (1:11–14), and ends with Israel freely building a house for God. The Hebrew word avodah means both "slavery" and "worship," and the book uses it for both (1:14; 12:25–26; 35:21, 24; 39:32, 42). The whole book might be summarized as a move from forced work for a king to willing work for God, with the Sabbath in between as the sign that Israel is no longer slaves. The contrast between Egypt's forced service and Israel's worship is also drawn by Fretheim, Sarna and Carol Meyers.

settings.what: The command to set up the tabernacle
settings.to: Moses
settings.when: For the first day of the first month, a year after the exodus
settings.why: To tell Moses to raise the tabernacle, set each furnishing in place, and anoint everything. He is to wash, dress and anoint Aaron and his sons, so that their anointing makes them priests for all time. The date makes it a new year, like a new creation.
settings.readers: For Israel this answered the question of God's presence that runs through the book. Moses does it all "as the LORD commanded," and then the glory fills the tent.
